verses.zh: 尼布甲尼撒王晓谕住在全地各方、各国、各族的人说：「愿你们大享平安！
verses.en: (3:31)[NOTE:1] King Nebuchadnezzar, to all peoples, nations, and language groups that live in all the land: “Peace and prosperity![NOTE:2]
notes: Beginning with 4:1, the verse numbers through 4:37 in the English Bible differ from the verse numbers in the Aramaic text (BHS), with 4:1 ET = 3:31 AT, 4:2 ET = 3:32 AT, 4:3 ET = 3:33 AT, 4:4 ET = 4:1 AT, etc., through 4:37 ET = 4:34 AT. Thus Dan 3:31-33 of the Aramaic text appears as Dan 4:1-3 in the English Bible, and the corresponding verses of ch. 4 differ accordingly. In spite of the division of the Aramaic text, a good case can be made that 3:31-33 AT (= 4:1-3 ET) is actually the introduction to ch. 4.
Aram “May your peace increase!”
verses.commentary:
4:1 "Nebuchadnezzar" Dan. 4:1-3 is in chapter 3 in the Hebrew Bible, but this context obviously
starts a new section. His name may mean "may Nebo guard the boundary" (cf. Dan. 4:8). See full note at Dan. 1:1.

▣ "all the peoples, nations, and men of every language" We must remember that the
kingdom of neo-Babylon included many language groups (cf. Dan. 3:4,7,29; 6:25). This chapter
seems to be a royal decree issued to praise the God of Judah for Nebuchadnezzar's restoration.

▣ "in all the earth" This, of course, refers to the known world of that day and is an example
of a non-literal exaggeration (hyperbole). See G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible,
pp. 22,110-117,121,133,181.

▣ "May your peace abound" This is parallel to Dan. 6:25 (cf. Ezra 4:17). This was a common
idiom for initial greetings, meaning "welfare," "prosperity" (BDB 1116). Nebuchadnezzar II is declaring, in
a royal decree, the praises of the God of Judah, who he calls "the Most High God" (BDB 1080, 1106 both with the
DEFINITE ARTICLE, see Hebrew form at BDB 43;
SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.).

verses.zh: 我乐意将至高的　神向我所行的神迹奇事宣扬出来。
verses.en: I am delighted to tell you about the signs and wonders that the most high God has done for me.
verses.commentary:
4:2 "the signs and wonders which the Most High God has done for me." Nebuchadnezzar II has now been
confronted with YHWH in chapters 2, 3, and 4. The accumulating evidence of the existence, sovereignty, and
covenant loyalty of the Jewish God is overwhelming.

The book of Daniel is characterized by lists and hendiadys. See the third paragraph of
Dan. 2:12. The corresponding Hebrew terms for "signs," and "wonders" are often used together
(cf. Exod. 7:3; 8:23; Deut. 4:34; 6:22; 7:19; 13:1,2; 26:8; 28:46; 29:3; 34:11; Neh. 9:10; Ps. 105:27;
135:9; Jer. 32:20). What God did for Israel in the Exodus (cf. Acts 7:36) He now displays to pagan kings
(Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, and Darius). The revelation continues in the life of Jesus (cf. Acts 2:22)
and the gospel proclamation (cf. Acts 2:43; 4:30; 5:12; 8:13; 14:3). However, in the NT these two terms
are usually associated with false Messiahs (cf. Matt. 24:24; Mark 13:22) or the Jewish people demanding
evidence of Jesus' Messiahship (cf. Matt. 12:39; 16:1; John 4:48). God wants the world to know Him!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIGN

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

verses.zh: 他的神迹何其大！他的奇事何其盛！他的国是永远的；他的权柄存到万代！
verses.en: “How great are his signs! How mighty are his wonders! His kingdom will last forever,[NOTE:1] and his authority continues from one generation to the next.”
notes: Aram “His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom.”
verses.commentary:
4:3 "His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom" This verse is a poetic/hymnic text extolling YHWH.

- "His signs. . .and wonders" (cf. Dan. 6:27). God is actively involved in the lives of these
Near Eastern kings (cf. chapters 2;3;4;5;6) to demonstrate His power and presence.

- "everlasting kingdom" (cf. Dan. 4:34; 2:44; 6:26; 7:14,26). This is in contrast to the changing
kingdom represented by the vision of chapter 2. These last two lines of poetry are very similar
to the Hebrew of Ps. 145:13; also see Ps. 45:6; Lam. 5:19.

- "dominion is from generation to generation." God's people are safe and secure in Him in each
and every generation, even amidst war and exile. Physical circumstances (destruction of Jerusalem
and the temple) do not affect the peace and presence of God in the lives of His followers. These
words and phrases are in a parallel relationship in Dan. 4:3. Semitic poetry must be interpreted
in light of thought parallels, not rhyme.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: IMMANUEL'S PERSON AND REIGN

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGDOM OF GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

verses.zh: 「我尼布甲尼撒安居在宫中，平顺在殿内。
verses.en: (4:1)[NOTE:1] I, Nebuchadnezzar, was relaxing in my home,[NOTE:2] living luxuriously[NOTE:3] in my palace.
notes: This verse marks the beginning of chap. 4 in the Aramaic text of Daniel (see the note on 4:1). The Greek OT (LXX) has the following addition: “In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign he said.” This date would suggest a link to the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 b.c. In general, the LXX of chapters 4-6 is very different from the MT, so much so that the following notes will call attention only to selected readings. In Daniel 4 the LXX lacks sizable portions of material in the MT (e.g., vv. 3-6, 31-32), includes sizable portions of material not in the MT (e.g., v. 14a, parts of vv. 16, 28), has a different order of some material (e.g., v. 8 after v. 9), and in some instances is vastly different from the MT (e.g., vv. 30, 34). Whether these differences are due to an excessively paraphrastic translation technique adopted for these chapters in the LXX, or are due to differences in the underlying Vorlage of the LXX, is a disputed matter. The latter seems more likely. There is a growing trend in modern scholarship to take the LXX of chapters 4-6 much more seriously than was the case in most earlier text-critical studies that considered this issue.
Aram “my house.”
Aram “happy.”
verses.commentary:
4:4

NASB
"was at ease in my house and flourishing in my palace"

NKJV
"was at rest in my house, and flourishing in my palace"

NRSV
"was living at ease in my home and prospering in my palace"

TEV
"was living comfortably in my palace"

NJB
"was living comfortably in my house, prosperously in my palace"

This is another example of Semitic parallelism (as is Dan. 4:5). Nebuchadnezzar II was
experiencing the kind of prosperity that he had wished for his hearers in Dan. 4:1.

This seems to be an allusion to the up-coming dream of a glorious tree. This type of human
arrogance is prophesied in Isa. 47:7,8. Isaiah 13-14 and 46-47 are oracles of judgment against Babylon,
which becomes the biblical symbol of human arrogance and pride (similar to the Tower of Babel and Edom).

verses.zh: 我做了一梦，使我惧怕。我在床上的思念，并脑中的异象，使我惊惶。
verses.en: I saw a dream that[NOTE:1] frightened me badly. The things I imagined while lying on my bed—these visions of my mind—were terrifying me.
notes: Aram “and it.”
verses.commentary:
4:5-7 Again the impotence of Neo-Babylon and its wise men is contrasted with the wise power and
control of the God of Judah and her people.

4:5 "I saw a dream. . .the visions in my mind" Dreams were often thought to be the gods revealing information to ANE
kings. Therefore, these rulers had to have people to interpret these revelations (biblical examples would be Joseph and
Daniel). For a good discussion of this cultural expectation, see John H. Walton, Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the
Old Testament: Introducing the Conceptual World of the Hebrew Bible, p. 243 and footnote #50.

▣ "fearful" There are two similar Aramaic roots for fear and dismay that are used often in Daniel, usually
connected to the visions.

- בהל (BDB 1084)

- "in haste" caused by fear ‒ Dan. 2:25; 3:24; 6:19

- fear caused by vision/dream ‒ Dan. 4:5,19; 5:6,10; 7:15,28

- דחל (BDB 1087)

- fear caused by a vision/dream ‒ Dan. 2:31; 4:5

- fear of Nebuchadnezzar's power ‒ Dan. 5:19

- part of Nebuchadnezzar's decree ‒ Dan. 6:26

- in description of the 4th beast ‒ Dan. 7:7,19

verses.zh: 所以我降旨召巴比伦的一切哲士到我面前，叫他们把梦的讲解告诉我。
verses.en: So I issued an order[NOTE:1] for all the wise men of Babylon to be brought[NOTE:2] before me so that they could make known to me the interpretation of the dream.
notes: Aram “from me there was placed a decree.”
The Aramaic infinitive here is active.
verses.commentary:
4:6 "So I gave orders" Nebuchadnezzar II can make decrees (cf. Dan. 2:9,15; 3:10,29), but he could
not produce the desired result (and neither could his wise men). This is in stark contrast to God's will
being accomplished (i.e., Isa. 55:9-11).

verses.zh: 于是那些术士、用法术的、迦勒底人、观兆的都进来，我将那梦告诉了他们，他们却不能把梦的讲解告诉我。
verses.en: When the magicians, astrologers, wise men, and diviners entered, I recounted the dream for them. But they were unable to make known its interpretation to me.
verses.commentary:
4:7 For the meaning of these terms see Dan. 1:20 or 2:2.

▣ "the Chaldeans" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

▣ "they could not make known its interpretation" It is unusual that they did not attempt an
interpretation, given the fact that Nebuchadnezzar II had revealed the dream. Possibly they would have attempted to
interpret it, but were afraid to.

It is surprising that Nebuchadnezzar II calls on the same group of wise men which he previously
had no confidence in (cf. Dan. 2:4-13), and also that he had forgotten his own decrees (Dan. 2:4-49; 3:29)
relating to YHWH. This seems to imply that several documents about Daniel circulated separately and were later combined.

Modern Bible scholars do not know who or when the final form of the OT books was decided. Believers
assume inspiration extends to editors and scribes.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

verses.zh: 末后那照我神的名，称为伯提沙撒的但以理来到我面前，他里头有圣神的灵，我将梦告诉他说：
verses.en: Later Daniel entered (whose name is Belteshazzar after the name of my god,[NOTE:1] and in whom there is a spirit of the holy gods). I recounted the dream for him as well,
notes: This explanation of the meaning of the name Belteshazzar may be more of a paronomasia than a strict etymology. See the note at 1:7. The king's god was Marduk, who was called Bel (“Lord”).
verses.commentary:
4:8 "Daniel" The name means "God is my judge" (BDB 1088). See full note at Dan. 1:6.

▣ "Belteshazzar" Daniel's name implies a Babylonian deity, "may_______ protect his life" (BDB 1084).
The Babylonian pantheon developed from the Sumerian pantheon. Originally deities were the patrons of
specific cities. The god, Marduk, was known as "lord." Bel was originally the patron god
of the city of Nippur, but came to be identified with Marduk, the pagan god of the city of Babylon
(i.e. Bel, cf Isa. 46:1; Jer. 50:2; 51:44). It is uncertain exactly which god is implied by Daniel's
name, but Marduk became the chief god of the city of Babylon. Although Bel looks to be a part of
Daniel's Babylonian name, it is not. Daniel 4:8 functions as a parenthesis explaining the name, Belteshazzar
(cf. NKJV, NRSV, TEV).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MARDUK

SPECIAL TOPIC: BEL

▣

NASB, NRSV
"a spirit of the holy gods"

NKJV
"the Spirit of the Holy God"

TEV, NJB, JPS, NEB, REB, Peshitta
"the spirit of the holy gods"

If this phrase is from a polytheist (cf. Dan. 4:8a; 5:11,14) then surely this is not
a reference to YHWH or His Spirit (the textual evidence is that the qualifying ADJECTIVE
"holy" is PLURAL, however, there is a Hebrew PLURAL equivalent in Josh. 24:19,
although the LXX translation implies that it does refer to YHWH and that Nebuchadnezzar was a believer).
The context (Dan. 4:9) implies that Nebuchadnezzar II remembered Daniel's previous help of dream interpretation
in chapter 2; if so, then this could be translated like the NKJV (cf. Dan. 4:9,18). Remember the consistent
theological emphasis is YHWH's power and control versus the Babylonian pantheon and government
(cf. Dan. 2:20-23).

"The spirit" would be understood as YHWH's influence in Daniel's giftedness
(cf. Dan. 2:27-28,30,47).

This Aramaic phrase is similar to the Hebrew phrase used of Joseph in Gen. 41:38. Both
Joseph and Daniel served pagan kings and interpreted their dreams by divine revelations.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOLY

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

verses.zh: 『术士的领袖伯提沙撒啊，因我知道你里头有圣神的灵，甚么奥秘的事都不能使你为难。现在要把我梦中所见的异象和梦的讲解告诉我。』
verses.en: saying, “Belteshazzar, chief of the magicians, in whom I know there to be a spirit of the holy gods and whom no mystery baffles, consider[NOTE:1] my dream that I saw and set forth its interpretation!
notes: The present translation assumes the reading חֲזִי (khazi, “consider”) rather than the MT חֶזְוֵי (khezve, “visions”). The MT implies that the king required Daniel to disclose both the dream and its interpretation, as in chapter 2. But in the following verses Nebuchadnezzar recounts his dream, while Daniel presents only its interpretation.
verses.commentary:
4:9 "the chief of the magicians" Daniel was trained in the language and traditions of the Chaldeans
(cf. Dan. 1:4). He was made the leader of the Babylonian wise men (cf. Dan. 1:20; 2:48). Daniel's abilities
were from YHWH, not from Babylonian magic. These Babylonian wise men failed again and again (cf. Dan. 2:1-13;
4:7,18). Daniel's position and title caused later Jewish rabbis to criticize his cooperation with pagan culture and
governments.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

▣

NASB
"tell me the vision"

NKJV
"explain to me the vision"

NRSV
"hear the dream"

TEV
"this is my dream"

NJB
"this is the dream"

REB, Peshitta
"tell me its interpretation"

From these English translations it is obvious there are at least two ways to interpret
the Aramaic text:

- Nebuchadnezzar II wanted Daniel to reveal the dream and its interpretation,
like chapter 2 (NASB, NKJV)

- Nebuchadnezzar II told Daniel the dream (as he did the other wise men, cf. Dan. 4:7
and NRSV, TEV, NJB) and wanted him to give the interpretation. The second makes sense
contextually, but demands a revocalization of the Masoretic Consonantal Text. The VOWEL
markings in the MT are a later addition and not inspired.

See UBS Text Project, vol. 5, pp. 204-205.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT (MT)

verses.zh: 「我在床上脑中的异象是这样：我看见地当中有一棵树，极其高大。
verses.en: Here are the visions of my mind[NOTE:1] while I was on my bed. “While I was watching,there was a tree in the middle of the land.[NOTE:2] It was enormously tall.[NOTE:3]
notes: The LXX lacks the first two words (Aram “the visions of my head”) of the Aramaic text.

Instead of “in the middle of the land,” some English versions render this phrase “a tree at the center of the earth” (NRSV); NAB, CEV “of the world”; NLT “in the middle of the earth.” The Hebrew phrase can have either meaning.
Aram “its height was great.”
verses.commentary:
4:10 "behold" A Handbook on the Book of Daniel, by UBS, pp. 106-107, notes that this
Aramaic interjection (BDB 1080) and its Hebrew equivalent (BDB 243) are used often in Daniel, but usually
not translated.

- Aramaic ‒ Dan. 2:31; 4:10,13; 7:2,5,7,8 (twice), 13

- Hebrew ‒ Dan. 8:3,5,15,19; 9:18; 10:5,10,16; 11:2; 12:5

Its literary function is to energize the narrative.

▣ "a tree" This was apparently a common symbol of the power and pervasiveness of important
men in the Ancient Near East (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 374, 2. e.; cf. Ezek. 17:3,22-24; 19:10-14; 31 and Herodotus 1.108; 7.19).

See a good brief article on the concept of "A cosmic tree at the center of the earth,"

- IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 736

- John H. Walton, ANE Thought and the OT, pp. 175-176

SPECIAL TOPIC: TREES

▣

NASB. NKJV, Peshitta
"in the midst of the earth"

NRSV, REB
"at the center of the earth"

TEV
"in the middle of the earth"

NJB
"in the middle of the world"

This is an idiomatic way of showing the extent and power of the neo-Babylon empire
(cf. Dan. 2:38-39; 4:20-22). As always interpreters must take this figurative (hyperbolic) language
in the sense it would have been used by a king in the ancient Near East. Nebuchadnezzar II controlled
the known world.

verses.zh: 那树渐长，而且坚固，高得顶天，从地极都能看见，
verses.en: The tree grew large and strong.Its top reached far into the sky;it could be seen[NOTE:1] from the borders of all the land.[NOTE:2]
notes: Aram “its sight,” as also v. 17.
Or “to the end of all the earth” (so KJV, ASV); NCV, CEV “from anywhere on earth.”
verses.commentary:
4:11 This verse has all PARTICIPLES, showing continuing action. The tree (kingdom)
was still expanding.

▣"its height reached to the sky" This phrase is reminiscent of the Tower of Babel in Gen. 11:4,
which also denotes human arrogance and pride (cf. Isa. 14:14).

▣ "it was visible to the end of the whole earth" This is obviously poetic hyperbole.

verses.zh: 叶子华美，果子甚多，可作众生的食物；田野的走兽卧在荫下，天空的飞鸟宿在枝上；凡有血气的都从这树得食。
verses.en: Its foliage was attractive and its fruit plentiful;on it there was food enough for all.Under it the wild animals[NOTE:1] used to seek shade,and in its branches the birds of the sky used to nest.All creatures[NOTE:2] used to feed themselves from it.
notes: Aram “the beasts of the field.”
Aram “all flesh.”
verses.commentary: 4:12 The neo-Babylonian empire provided a safe and growing economic climate.

verses.zh: 「我在床上脑中的异象，见有一位守望的圣者从天而降。
verses.en: “While I was watching in my mind’s visions[NOTE:1] on my bed,a holy sentinel[NOTE:2] came down from heaven.
notes: Aram “the visions of my head.”

Aram “a watcher and a holy one.” The expression is a hendiadys, as also in v. 23. This “watcher” is apparently an angel. The Greek OT (LXX) in fact has ἄγγελος (angelos, “angel”) here. Theodotion simply transliterates the Aramaic word (ʿir). The term is sometimes rendered “sentinel” (NAB) or “messenger” (NIV, NLT).
verses.commentary:
4:13 "the angelic watcher" This means "one that stays awake" (BDB 1105). The Hebrew counterpart
is used of God in Ps. 121:4. This Aramaic word and concept is used only in this chapter in the entire
Bible. It is SINGULAR in Dan. 4:13 but PLURAL in 4:17. The Hebrew counterpart is used

- of angels in the inter-testamental books of Jubilees (4:15) and I Enoch (1:5)

- for fallen angels (cf. I Enoch 10-16)

- It has been found in Cave 1 of the Qumran Text in "the Genesis Apocraphon" and is used for fallen angels (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEMONS [fallen angels]).

- It is also known to be the title for the messenger of the gods in the Canaanite pantheon (Ras Shamra texts from Ugarit).

We are uncertain if this is an allusion to Babylonian mythology or simply a unique way to refer to a special type of
angel who kept watch over "the cosmic tree." For a good brief article on "watchers," see IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 736.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

▣ "a holy one" Nebuchadnezzar II recognized that "the watcher" was a single being from the divine realm
(hendiadys). We must be careful of putting too much weight on the words of a pagan king, who was a polytheist and wordshiped
Marduk.

This "holy one" declared the divine judgment on Nebuchadnezzar II (for a period of time). Angels serve to
implement God's will.

- revelation

- judgment

- deliverance

- restoration

- protection

It is interesting that Millard Erickson, in his Christian Theology 2nd ed., p. 462, asserts
that the collective term "angels" is made up of

- "sons of the Elohim" (Job 1:6; 2:1,6; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.)

- "sons of Elim" (Ps. 29:1; 89:6)

- "holy ones" (Ps. 89:5,7)

- "watchers" (Dan. 4:13,17,23)

- "the council" (Ps. 89:7)

- "the assembly" (Ps. 89:5)

- "host of heaven," used many times; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: godly ones, holy ones

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

▣ "descended from heaven" Since the word "heaven" is also used in Dan. 4:11b, however in a
different sense, this is a good opportunity to emphasize the crucial aspect of context in interpretation.
Lexicons and dictionaries do not give meaning, only literary (or verbal) contexts give meaning. In 4:11 the
term refers to the sky (cf. Dan. 4:15d, see
SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN), but in
Dan. 4:13 (cf. 4:26-31, see SPECIAL
TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN) it refers to the dwelling place of God or the gods.

verses.zh: 大声呼叫说：『伐倒这树！砍下枝子！摇掉叶子！抛散果子！使走兽离开树下，飞鸟躲开树枝。
verses.en: He called out loudly[NOTE:1] as follows:[NOTE:2] ‘Chop down the tree and lop off its branches!Strip off its foliageand scatter its fruit!Let the animals flee from under itand the birds from its branches.
notes: Aram “in strength.”
Aram “and thus he was saying.”
verses.commentary:
4:14 "He shouted out" Apparently the reader is meant to understand that one of the holy watchers
cried out to the other angelic beings (cf. Dan. 4:17). Remember, however, this is a highly symbolic and
figurative dream, not time-space reality.

verses.zh: 树墩却要留在地内，用铁圈和铜圈箍住，在田野的青草中让天露滴湿，使他与地上的兽一同吃草，
verses.en: But leave its taproot[NOTE:1] in the ground,with a band of iron and bronze around it[NOTE:2] surrounded by the grass of the field.Let it become damp with the dew of the sky,and let it live with[NOTE:3] the animals in the grass of the land.
notes: Aram “the stock of its root,” as also in v. 23. The implication here is that although the tree is chopped down, it is not killed. Its life-giving root is spared. The application to Nebuchadnezzar is obvious.

The function of the band of iron and bronze is not entirely clear, but it may have had to do with preventing the splitting or further deterioration of the portion of the tree that was left after being chopped down. By application it would then refer to the preservation of Nebuchadnezzar’s life during the time of his insanity.
Aram “its lot be.”
verses.commentary:
4:15 "a band of iron" There has been much discussion about the band.

- Most commentators assume that it was for the protection of the stump.

- Although some see it as being related to the restraints that bound Nebuchadnezzar II during the time that he was deranged.

- The LXX sees it as referring to the king himself as a symbol of his restoration to the throne.

The tree stands for the kingship of Nebuchadnezzar II. God cuts down/brings down his kingdom
(cf. Isa. 10:33-34; Ezek. 17:22-24). However, the stump remains and will regenerate.

This imagery is also used of the stump of Jesse (i.e., the Messiah, cf. Isa. 11:1; 53:2; Jer. 23:5; 33:15). This is
the origin of the Messianic term "Branch" (i.e., netzer, cf. Isa. 4:2; Zech. 3:8; 6:12).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BRANCH OF THE LORD

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS THE NAZARENE

▣

NASB
"let him share with the beasts in the grass of the earth"

NKJV
"let him graze with the beasts on the grass of the earth"

NRSV
"let his lot be with the animals of the field in the grass of the earth"

TEV
"let him live with the animals and the plants"

NJB
"have its lot with the animals, eating grass"

As you can tell by these English translations, there are two ways to understand this
ambiguous phrase.

- The king will live outdoors in the royal gardens with the domestic animals (NASB, NRSV, TEV).

- The king will eat grass like the domestic animals (NKJV, NJB).

verses.zh: 使他的心改变，不如人心；给他一个兽心，使他经过七期（期：或译年；本章同）。
verses.en: Let his mind[NOTE:1] be altered from that of a human being,and let an animal’s mind be given to him,and let seven periods of time[NOTE:2] go by for[NOTE:3] him.
notes: Aram “its heart.” The metaphor of the tree begins to fade here and the reality behind the symbol (the king) begins to emerge.
The seven periods of time probably refer to seven years.
Aram “over” (also in vv. 23, 25, 32).
verses.commentary:
4:16 "Let his mind" This word is literally "heart," which in Hebrew was imagery for the mental
processes and choices of the person.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

▣

NASB
"And let seven periods of time pass over him"

NKJV, NRSV
"let seven times pass over him"

TEV
"for seven years"

NJB, REB
"seven times shall pass over him"

Peshitta
"and let seven seasons change over him"

This phrase becomes theologically significant because

- the term "seven" is used both literally and figuratively in the Bible (see
SPECIAL
TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #4). In Hebrew thought it is the perfect number going
back to the consummation of creation week of Genesis 1 (i.e., the day God rested).

- the term "time" is used in several of the prophecies of Daniel. Is it referring to a specific
period of time or a full or perfect period of time? These possibilities must be answered from context,
not philology or lexicology.

The LXX has "seven years," but the term implies "seasons," "annual seasons." The time
element is divinely set and known but recorded for us in a purposefully ambiguous way.

verses.zh: 这是守望者所发的命，圣者所出的令，好叫世人知道至高者在人的国中掌权，要将国赐与谁就赐与谁，或立极卑微的人执掌国权。』
verses.en: This announcement is by the decree of the sentinels;this decision is by the pronouncement of the holy ones, so that[NOTE:1] those who are alive may understand that the Most High has authority over human kingdoms,[NOTE:2] and he bestows them on whomever he wishes.He establishes over them even the lowliest of human beings.’
notes: The present translation follows an underlying reading of עַל־דִּבְרַת (ʿal divrat, “so that”) rather than MT עַד־דִּבְרַת (ʿad divrat, “until”).
Aram “the kingdom of man”; NASB “the realm of mankind”; NCV “every kingdom on earth.”
verses.commentary:
4:17 "This sentence is by the decree of the angelic watchers,

And the decision is a command of the holy ones" This
seems to imply that the angels made the decision on their own, but Dan. 4:24 shows the ultimate source
of this decision was the Most High God. Again, it is important to realize that the Jews were uncertain at this time about
their covenant relationship with YHWH because the temple and Jerusalem (cf. Deut. 12:10) had been destroyed
and the Davidic king taken into exile (cf. 2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17). They needed Him to show them that He was in control
of all of world history.

The concluding part of this verse is very similar in theological emphasis to Dan. 2:20. The
entire book of Daniel makes this assertion again and again. To the Ancient Near East the historical
situation looked as if YHWH had been defeated by the Babylonian gods, but in reality YHWH was using the
empires of the Fertile Crescent (Assyria, Babylon, Persia) to execute His will related to His people
(cf. Isa. 10:5; Jer. 51:20). God's people were reaping the consequences of idolatry and rebellion
(cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-29). God needed to reassure His people and inform the pagan empires (Dan. 4:25) of
the source of their current political and military prowess (i.e., Dan. 2:21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: godly ones, holy ones

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

verses.zh: 「这是我―尼布甲尼撒王所做的梦。伯提沙撒啊，你要说明这梦的讲解；因为我国中的一切哲士都不能将梦的讲解告诉我，惟独你能，因你里头有圣神的灵。」
verses.en: “This is the dream that I, King Nebuchadnezzar, saw. Now you, Belteshazzar, declare its[NOTE:1] interpretation, for none of the wise men in[NOTE:2] my kingdom are able to make known to me the interpretation. But you can do so, for a spirit of the holy gods is in you.”
notes: The present translation, as also in the next verse, reads פִּשְׁרֵהּ (pishreh, “its interpretation”) with the Qere and many medieval Hebrew MSS; the Kethib is פִּשְׁרָא (pishraʾ, “the interpretation”).
Aram “of.”
verses.commentary:
4:18 "This is the dream. . .tell me its interpretation" In the ANE dreams and visions were often used to communicate
divine messages to humans. Two good articles are:

- John H. Walton, ANE Thought and the OT, p. 243

- NIDOTTE, vol. 3, pp. 721-724

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣ "inasmuch as none of the wise men of my kingdom is able" This is a recurrent theme
(cf. Dan. 1:20; 2:4-13; 4:7; 5:7-8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVINATION

verses.zh: 于是称为伯提沙撒的但以理惊讶片时，心意惊惶。王说：「伯提沙撒啊，不要因梦和梦的讲解惊惶。」伯提沙撒回答说：「我主啊，愿这梦归与恨恶你的人，讲解归与你的敌人。
verses.en: Then Daniel (whose name is also Belteshazzar) was upset for a brief time;[NOTE:1] his thoughts were alarming him. The king said, “Belteshazzar, don’t let the dream and its interpretation alarm you.” But Belteshazzar replied, “Sir,[NOTE:2] if only the dream were for your enemies and its interpretation applied to your adversaries!
notes: Aram “about one hour.” The expression refers idiomatically to a brief period of time of undetermined length.
Aram “my lord.”
verses.commentary:
4:19 "Daniel. . .was appalled for a while" Daniel was apparently very loyal to Nebuchadnezzar II and
regretted having to reveal this judgment. Several times in the book of Daniel, Daniel is spiritually and
physically affected by the revelations he receives (cf. Dan. 7:15,28; 8:27; 10:16,17).

It seems that "appalled" and "alarmed" are parallel grammatical structures so characteristic
of the book of Daniel.

▣ "do not let the dream or its interpretation alarm you" Nebuchadnezzar II had himself been
alarmed by this dream (cf. Dan. 4:5).

▣ "those who hate you. . .to your adversaries" This is another of many parallel phrases. This
literary style characterizes the entire book (cf. Dan. 4:21c,d, and e,f; 22a,b; 23c,d).

verses.zh: 你所见的树渐长，而且坚固，高得顶天，从地极都能看见；
verses.en: The tree that you saw that grew large and strong, whose top reached to the sky, and that could be seen[NOTE:1] in all the land,
notes: Aram “its sight.”

verses.zh: 叶子华美，果子甚多，可作众生的食物；田野的走兽住在其下；天空的飞鸟宿在枝上。
verses.en: whose foliage was attractive and its fruit plentiful, and from which there was food available for all, under whose branches wild animals[NOTE:1] used to live, and in whose branches birds of the sky used to nest—
notes: Aram “the beasts of the field” (also in vv. 23, 25, 32).

verses.zh: 「王啊，这渐长又坚固的树就是你。你的威势渐长及天，你的权柄管到地极。
verses.en: it is you,[NOTE:1] O king! For you have become great and strong. Your greatness is such that it reaches to heaven and your authority to the ends of the earth.
notes: Much of modern scholarship views this chapter as a distortion of traditions that were originally associated with Nabonidus rather than with Nebuchadnezzar. A Qumran text, the Prayer of Nabonidus, is often cited for parallels to these events.
verses.commentary:
4:22 "it is you, O king" The king himself as the representative of his empire is the focus of the
dream, as in Daniel 2 (2:38b, "you are the head of gold").

verses.zh: 王既看见一位守望的圣者从天而降，说：『将这树砍伐毁坏，树墩却要留在地内，用铁圈和铜圈箍住；在田野的青草中，让天露滴湿，使他与地上的兽一同吃草，直到经过七期。』
verses.en: As for the king seeing a holy sentinel coming down from heaven and saying, ‘Chop down the tree and destroy it, but leave its taproot in the ground, with a band of iron and bronze around it, surrounded by the grass of the field. Let it become damp with the dew of the sky, and let it live with the wild animals, until seven periods of time go by for him’—

verses.zh: 「王啊，讲解就是这样：临到我主我王的事是出于至高者的命。
verses.en: this is the interpretation, O king. It is the decision of the Most High that this has happened to my lord the king.

verses.zh: 你必被赶出离开世人，与野地的兽同居，吃草如牛，被天露滴湿，且要经过七期。等你知道至高者在人的国中掌权，要将国赐与谁就赐与谁。
verses.en: You will be driven[NOTE:1] from human society,[NOTE:2] and you will live[NOTE:3] with the wild animals. You will be fed[NOTE:4] grass like oxen,[NOTE:5] and you will become damp with the dew of the sky. Seven periods of time will pass by for you before[NOTE:6] you understand that the Most High is ruler over human kingdoms and gives them to whomever he wishes.
notes: The Aramaic indefinite active plural is used here like the English passive, as also in vv. 28, 29, and 32.
Aram “from mankind,” as also in v. 32.
Aram “your dwelling will be,” as also in v. 32.
Or perhaps: “be made to eat.”

Nebuchadnezzar’s insanity has features that are associated with the mental disorder boanthropy, in which the person so afflicted imagines himself to be an ox or a similar animal and behaves accordingly.
Aram “until.”
verses.commentary:
4:25 "until you recognize that the Most High is ruler over the realm of mankind, and bestows it on
whomever He wishes" See full note at Dan. 4:17. This is the central and recurrent theme of Daniel
(cf. Ps. 83:18; 97:9; Jer. 27:5; Romans 9-11).

The LXX adds a temporal note at the beginning of this chapter and chapter 3 ("in the
eighteenth year"). This would designate the year that Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed.
Nebuchadnezzar II needed to recognize YHWH's permission for his apparent victory (i.e., Dan. 2:21).

verses.zh: 守望者既吩咐存留树墩，等你知道诸天掌权，以后你的国必定归你。
verses.en: They said to leave the taproot of the tree, for your kingdom will be restored to you when you come to understand that heaven[NOTE:1] rules.
notes: The reference to heaven here is a circumlocution for God. There was a tendency in Jewish contexts to avoid direct reference to God. Compare the expression “kingdom of heaven” in the NT and such statements as: “I have sinned against heaven and in your sight” (Luke 15:21).
verses.commentary:
4:26

NASB
"it is Heaven that rules"

NKJV
"Heaven rules"

NRSV
"Heaven is sovereign"

TEV
"God rules all the world"

NJB
"the Most HIgh rules over human sovereignty"

Peshitta
"that authority is from heaven"

This is a circumlocution, a way of referring to deity without using a title/name
(cf. Matt. 3:2, "kingdom of heaven"; and Luke 15:18,21, "sinned against heaven").

verses.zh: 王啊，求你悦纳我的谏言，以施行公义断绝罪过，以怜悯穷人除掉罪孽，或者你的平安可以延长。」
verses.en: Therefore, O king, may my advice be pleasing to you. Break away from your sins by doing what is right, and from your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor. Perhaps your prosperity will be prolonged.”[NOTE:1]
notes: Aram “if there may be a lengthening to your prosperity.”
verses.commentary:
4:27 Daniel's advice to Nebuchadnezzar recognizes the biblical worldview (OT) that there is a
holy God who requires righteousness. These words to a proud eastern monarch shows the basic ethical
nature of reality. Kings were meant to act for the welfare of the people.

Sin and rebellion are the problem, but God is a God of mercy (cf. Isa. 55:6-7; Ezek. 18:21-22).
These words to Nebuchadnezzar II show Daniel's understanding that pagans are loved by God and can respond
to Him by faith and life. However, these kings will be judged for their actions.

These revelatory words of potential judgment to the Neo-Babylonian King who destroyed Jerusalem and
the temple, would have encourage the exiled covenant people. World empires are subject to Israel's God (cf. Dan. 2:21).
Even pagan rulers are called on to show mercy and fairness to their subjects.

The parallelism of "sins" and "iniquities" is obvious, but also "righteousness" and "mercy
to the poor" are parallel. This reflects the Jewish understanding of almsgiving (in the LXX translation
as well as usage in the Aramaic Targums and Talmud, cf. Ps. 112:3,9; Isa. 33:15; Matt. 6:1; 2 Cor. 9:6-11) as an
expression of "righteousness" (i.e. God's character, cf. Isa. 58:6-11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALMSGIVING

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

▣

NASB
"break away"

NKJV
"break off"

NRSV
"atone for"

NJB
"break with"

LXX
"redeem"

Peshitta
"get rid of"

This is literally "tear off" or "break off" (BDB 1108, Peal IMPERATIVE,
cf. Gen. 27:40). Humans have been given a free will. They must exercise it for righteousness, not self.
There are pivotal moments of appropriate choices and accompanying actions. Seize the moral moment! Current
choices determine future conditions.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "in case there may be a prolonging of your prosperity" YHWH is warning a proud ANE king to change his ways. The hope
would be that he would be spared from judgment. This is very similar to the revelatory word by Jonah that changed the King of Niveveh's
ways.

Repentance and faith make a difference! This was even true for the evil King Manassah, who repented and believed
at the very end of a terrible reign (cf. 2 Chr. 33:18-20).

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT

verses.zh: 这事都临到尼布甲尼撒王。
verses.en: Now all this happened[NOTE:1] to King Nebuchadnezzar.
notes: Aram “reached.”
verses.commentary:
4:28 This summary verse is placed first, similar to Dan. 4:1-3. This verse asserts a great biblical
truth—what God says comes to be (cf. Numbers 23:19c; Isa. 40:8; 45:23; 55:11). When all is said and
done, humanity's only hope is in the unchanging merciful character of God (cf. Mal. 3:6, see
SPECIAL TOPIC:
CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD [OT]). His promises are an extension of His character.

The theological difficulty of God's Sovereignty and human free will meet in the concept of covenant.
As far as God's promises of redemption, the covenant promises are "unconditional" (one example, "Gen. 15:12-21).

However, on an individual basis, His promises are "conditional" (see Deut. 30:15,19). Often Scripture clearly
expresses this by "If. . .then," but if when it is not stated it is implied.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ELECTION/PREDESTINATION AND LTHE NEED FOR A THEOLOGICAL BALANCE

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

verses.zh: 过了十二个月，他游行在巴比伦王宫里（原文是上）。
verses.en: After 12 months, he happened to be walking around on the battlements[NOTE:1] of the royal palace of Babylon.
notes: The word “battlements” is not in the text but is supplied from context. Many English versions supply “roof” here (e.g., NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV); cf. NLT “on the flat roof.”
verses.commentary:
4:29 "he was walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon" The people of the ANE used the roof
in the summertime as a cool place to rest and sleep.

verses.zh: 他说：「这大巴比伦不是我用大能大力建为京都，要显我威严的荣耀吗？」
verses.en: The king uttered these words: “Is this not the great Babylon that I have built for a royal residence[NOTE:1] by my own mighty strength[NOTE:2] and for my majestic honor?”
notes: Aram “house.”
Aram “by the might of my strength.”
verses.commentary:
4:30 "The king reflected and said" Pride has always been the major problem of fallen humanity
(cf. Genesis 3; Isaiah 14; Ezekiel 28; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: LIFTED UP).
This king had much to be proud of, as he is known from the Babylonian Archives as a great builder. Babylon's
Hanging Gardens were one of the Seven Wonders of the World. The city itself had huge double walls. The inner
wall of the city was 21 feet thick, 50 cubits high with towers every 60 feet. The outer wall was 11 feet
thick, 42 miles in circumference, and 6 feet beyond the outer wall was a man-made moat, which channeled
the waters of the Euphrates around the city for protection.

The LXX is very different from the MT in Daniel, chapters 4-6. At this point in the LXX the
arrogant king walking on the walls of his palace in the city of Babylon is King Nabonidus, Belshazzar's father
(cf. Dan. 5). The Dead Sea Scrolls 4Q242 records Nabonidus' illness and recovering after 7 years. It is
entitled "Prayer of Nabonidus."

▣ "by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty" Several of these words are used
in Dan. 2:37, where Nebuchadnezzar's possession of these is directly attributed to the God of Judah. All
he has is a gift from God, but he thinks it is all from himself (cf. Dan. 4:26,31,32; 2:37,44). Israel is warned
of this very attitude in Deuteronomy 8.

verses.zh: 这话在王口中尚未说完，有声音从天降下，说：「尼布甲尼撒王啊，有话对你说，你的国位离开你了。
verses.en: While these words were still on the king’s lips,[NOTE:1] a voice came down from heaven: “It is hereby announced to you,[NOTE:2] King Nebuchadnezzar, that your kingdom has been removed from you!
notes: Aram “in the mouth of the king.”
Aram “to you they say.”
verses.commentary:
4:31 "a voice came from heaven" The rabbis assumed that this is the Bath-kol of the
inter-biblical period, God's way of confirming His will during that time when there were no prophets
in Israel. But, in context, it seems to refer to the decree of the angelic watchers (cf. Dan. 4:13,23).

verses.zh: 你必被赶出离开世人，与野地的兽同居，吃草如牛，且要经过七期。等你知道至高者在人的国中掌权，要将国赐与谁就赐与谁。」
verses.en: You will be driven from human society, and you will live with the wild animals. You will be fed grass like oxen, and seven periods of time will pass by for you before[NOTE:1] you understand that the Most High is ruler over human kingdoms and gives them to whomever he wishes.”
notes: Aram “until.”
verses.commentary:
4:32-33 "Immediately the word concerning Nebuchadnezzar was fulfilled" If we see this as a psychological illness, his
malady is called lycantrophy or boanthrophy (cf. R. K. Harrison's Introduction to the OT, pp. 1115-1117).

There is even some historical documentation supporting Nebuchadnezzar's period of madness.

- Berossus (priest of Bel who wrote three history books about Babylon in Greek in the
fourth and third centuries B.C.). This tradition is recorded by Josephus
(Against Apion 1.19-20).

- Eusebius, Praep. Evang. IX.41, preserves the testimony of Abydenus (second century
B.C.) that Nebuchadnezzar, in his last days, was possessed by some god or other
(cf. R. K. Harrison, Introduction to the Old Testament, p. 1115).

It is also possible to try to connect this imagery to Sumerian myths related to the physical conditions
of primative humans (i.e., no regular food, shelter, or other privileges of civilization).

The exact time and nature of Nebuchadnezzar's condition is the fact God set the conditions
of his judgment. YHWH controls world events and powers!

▣ "his body was drenched with the dew of heaven" The temperature range in this part of the
earth is 120 degrees in summer to below freezing in winter. One can imagine the physical changes which
occurred in this man's body as he lived outdoors the year round.

verses.zh: 当时这话就应验在尼布甲尼撒的身上，他被赶出离开世人，吃草如牛，身被天露滴湿，头发长长，好像鹰毛；指甲长长，如同鸟爪。
verses.en: Now in that very moment[NOTE:1] this pronouncement about[NOTE:2] Nebuchadnezzar came true.[NOTE:3] He was driven from human society, he ate grass like oxen, and his body became damp with the dew of the sky, until his hair became long like an eagle’s feathers and his nails like a bird’s claws.[NOTE:4]
notes: Aram “hour.”
Or “on.”
Aram “was fulfilled.”
The words “feathers” and “claws” are not present in the Aramaic text, but have been added in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 日子满足，我―尼布甲尼撒举目望天，我的聪明复归于我，我便称颂至高者，赞美尊敬活到永远的　神。他的权柄是永有的；他的国存到万代。
verses.en: But at the end of the appointed time[NOTE:1] I, Nebuchadnezzar, looked up[NOTE:2] toward heaven, and my sanity returned to me.I extolled the Most High, and I praised and glorified the one who lives forever. For his authority is an everlasting authority, and his kingdom extends from one generation to the next.
notes: Aram “days.”
Aram “lifted up my eyes.”
verses.commentary:
4:34 "at the end of that period" This refers to the specific time mentioned in Dan. 4:16, "seven
periods of time." Most commentators think it refers to years, but this is speculation. However, the
specificity confirms that God is in control of Nebuchadnezzar's condition and healing.

The phrase "at that time" of v. 36, also denotes a specific time appointed by the Most High God. Israel's
God is in control of history!

▣ "I, Nebuchadnezzar, raised my eyes toward heaven" This is a symbolic way of referring to
his acknowledging Israel's God (cf. Dan. 4:36) and His sovereignty (cf. Dan. 4:34-35). As Nebuchadnezzar II "honored"
YHWH, the opposite is true of Belshazzar in Dan. 5:22-23.

▣ "Him who lives forever" This seems to be a play on the name "YHWH" from the Hebrew
VERB "to be" (cf. Exod. 3: 14). This theological affirmation is made several times in
Daniel (cf. Dan. 4:34; 6:26; 12:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR
DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

▣ "His dominion" This poetic theological affirmation is parallel to Dan. 4:3, as well as 2:44;
6:26-27. YHWH's Kingdom is eternal (cf. Dan. 7:14). The four kingdoms of Daniel 2 will pass away, but not
the Kingdom of the Most High!

verses.zh: 世上所有的居民都算为虚无；在天上的万军和世上的居民中，他都凭自己的意旨行事。无人能拦住他手，或问他说，你做甚么呢？
verses.en: All the inhabitants of the earth are regarded as nothing.[NOTE:1] He does as he wishes with the army of heavenand with those who inhabit the earth.No one slaps[NOTE:2] his handand says to him, “What have you done?”
notes: The present translation reads כְּלָא (kelaʾ), with many medieval Hebrew MSS, rather than כְּלָה (kelah) of BHS.
Aram “strikes against.”
verses.commentary:
4:35 This chapter has several poetic hymnic affirmations (cf. Dan. 4:3,34-35,37).

▣ "All the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing" This is not asserting that God
does not love humanity (i.e., John 3:16 and Special Topic below), but that no human individual or nation can compare
with God's power, authority, and longevity (cf. Isa. 40:17; Jer. 10:10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "the host of heaven" This phrase can have two orientations

- in texts relating to faithful Israel it refers to YHWH, the commander of the heavenly army of angels
(cf. Josh. 5:14-15; 1 Kgs. 22:19; Ps. 103:20-21)

- in texts which relate to Mesopotamian empires, particularly Babylon, who advocate and use astrology
or to idolatrous Israel, then it refers to YHWH as creator (cf. Gen. 1:14-19) and controller of the heavenly bodies
(sun, moon, stars, etc., e.g. Deut. 4:19; 17:3; 2 Kgs. 17:16; Ps. 33:6; Isa. 34:4; 40:26;
Jer. 8:2-3; 19:13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

▣ "And no one can ward off His hand" This word refers to child training or discipline. It is
a strong emphasis on God's sovereignty over all humans and nations (cf. Dan. 2:21; Isa. 43:13).

▣ "Or say to Him, 'What have You done'" This is another possible allusion to Isaiah
(cf. Isa. 10:15; 45:9-13). The phrase is imagery often related to making pottery (cf. Isa. 29:16;
Jer. 18; Rom. 9:19-22). God's total sovereignty is a recurrent theme (i.e., 2 Chr. 20:6; Job 9:12).

verses.zh: 那时，我的聪明复归于我，为我国的荣耀、威严，和光耀也都复归于我；并且我的谋士和大臣也来朝见我。我又得坚立在国位上，至大的权柄加增于我。
verses.en: At that time my sanity returned to me. I was restored[NOTE:1] to the honor of my kingdom, and my splendor returned to me. My ministers and my nobles were seeking me out, and I was reinstated[NOTE:2] over my kingdom. I became even greater than before.
notes: The translation reads הַדְרֵת (hadret, “I returned”) rather than the MT הַדְרִי (hadri, “my honor”); cf. Theodotion.
The translation reads הָתְקְנֵת (hotqenet, “I was established”) rather than the MT הָתְקְנַת (hotqenat, “it was established”). The MT could read: “And regarding my kingdom, it was established.”

verses.zh: 现在我―尼布甲尼撒赞美、尊崇、恭敬天上的王；因为他所做的全都诚实，他所行的也都公平。那行动骄傲的，他能降为卑。
verses.en: Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and exalt and glorify the King of heaven, for all his deeds are right and his ways are just. He is able to bring down those who live[NOTE:1] in pride.
notes: Aram “walk.”
verses.commentary:
4:37 "praise, exalt and honor" As is characteristic of Daniel several synonymous terms are used
to make a strong emphasis.

▣ "the King of heaven" This is a title related to the concept of YHWH as king of the universe
(cf. Jdgs. 8:23; 1 Sam. 8:7; Ps. 5:2; 29:10; 44:4; 47:6-8; 48:2; 68:24; 74:12; 84:3; 95:3; 97:1; 99:4;
146:10; Isa. 41:21; 43:15; 44:6; 52:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KINGDOM OF GOD

▣ "all His works are true and His ways just" Truth and justice are twin characteristics of
YHWH (cf. Deut. 32:4; Ps. 33:4-5). The one true God reveals knowledge and acts fairly. He wants His people
to emulate His character.

▣ "to humble those who walk in pride" This first refers to Nebuchadnezzar II (and Belshazzar,
cf. Dan. 5:20), but also to all Gentile empires represented by the image of four metals in chapter 2
(cf. Exod. 18:11). This is another common biblical theme (cf. Job 40:11-12; James 4:6,10; 2 Pet. 5:5-6).

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHT

- The verse numbering differs from translation to translation because Dan. 4:1-3 in the NASB is 3:31-33 in the
original Aramaic text.

- There are several recurrent themes

- praise of YHWH

- dream interpretation by YHWH

- sovereignty of YHWH

- There are many differences between the MT (Masoretic Text) and the LXX (Septuagint) in Daniel,
chapters 4-6.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT (MT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT (LXX)

- This chapter seems to be a very Jewish theological document. It has long been disputed that
a pagan polytheist like Nebuchadnezzar II could compose a chapter like this by himself (this
chapter is in the FIRST PERSON SINGULAR except for the period of Nebuchadnezzar's
madness). It is obvious from the book of Esther that King Ahasuerus (Xerxes I) allowed both Haman
and Mordecai to compose documents of their own in his name. Daniel is the Jewish theological
influence behind this chapter.

- Some of the specific reasons for why Nebuchadnezzar II could not have written this chapter are

- theological content, Dan. 4:3

- the style is in line with the rest of the book of Daniel

- Nebuchadnezzar is spoken of in the third person, Dan. 4:25-30

- Dan. 4:29 seems to be written for non-Babylonian people

- W.A. Criswell and E. J. Young assert that Nebuchadnezzar II is converted to the worship of
YHWH because of this final, great sign of Daniel 4. However, because of Dan. 4:8, it is obvious
to me that although he was greatly impressed, he was not willing to convert to the monotheism
of Israel. All known Babylonian documents of the period refer to him as a worshiper of Marduk.
